Render the objects and read them — that is the payload the API receives. Then apply. Then verify reconciliation separately through status and events.
Reviewing a values file is not reviewing a change: the template between them can do anything.

front: A Deployment exceeds progressDeadlineSeconds. What happens?
back:
It sets Progressing=False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded. That is all.
It does not roll back, does not stop retrying, and does not remediate. The deadline is status evidence, not a policy — treating it as automatic recovery is how a stalled rollout stays stalled overnight.

front: Server-Side Apply returns a field conflict. What is the safest reading?
back:
Another manager owns that field, and the API is telling you who. Read managedFields and decide deliberately.
Force transfers ownership — right when ownership is genuinely moving, wrong when a controller will simply set the value back. It is not a generic retry.

front: Minimum evidence for a stalled rollout
back:
• Deployment conditions and current revision
  • Desired / current / available counts on both ReplicaSets
  • Pod readiness and events
  • maxSurge and maxUnavailable arithmetic
  • managedFields or admission errors if updates were rejected

front: A Pod creation returns Forbidden: exceeded quota. Where do you look?
back:
At the rejected API request — not the scheduler. Quota is enforced at admission, so the object was never stored.
There is no Pod to describe and nothing Pending. Forbidden and Pending are different boundaries.

front: Why can adding a LimitRange make previously valid Pods fail quota?
back:
The LimitRange injects default requests or limits, and quota evaluates the object as admitted, not as submitted.
Those defaults count against the budget. The submitted YAML is unchanged — what changed is what the namespace says it means.

front: What a ResourceQuota can and cannot constrain
back:
Can: declared API resources — requests, limits — and object counts.
Cannot: actual runtime utilisation, which is a metrics and cgroup concern admission cannot see.
A namespace can sit at 100% of quota while its Pods are idle.

front: An in-place resize is accepted but status says deferred. What does that mean?
back:
Desired and actuated resources are separate. The API stored your request; the kubelet has not applied it — typically for lack of node capacity right now.
An accepted patch is never proof the cgroup changed. Read the resize status, not the spec.

front: Does an in-place resize change a Pod's QoS class?
back:
No. The class is fixed for the Pod's lifetime, which keeps its scheduling and eviction semantics stable.
A different class requires a replacement Pod. Resizing is not a route to Guaranteed.

front: What is the real trade of externalTrafficPolicy: Local?
back:
It preserves the client source address and avoids an extra hop — and it changes endpoint eligibility: only node-local endpoints are used.
A node with no local endpoint will not serve the traffic at all. It is a behaviour change, not a performance hint.

front: A LoadBalancer shows an ingress address. What is still unproven?
back:
Backend health, correct Service ports, non-empty and ready EndpointSlices, endpoint eligibility under traffic policy, and the Pod's own listener and policy.
Provisioning succeeded. That is the only claim the address makes.

front: A Service has EndpointSlices but serves no traffic. What is still unknown?
back:
Membership is not eligibility. Check the ready / serving / terminating conditions, the IP family and port, and whether traffic policy or locality excludes every endpoint on the receiving node.
Presence in a slice says an address exists, not that anything will use it.

front: Strict locality versus preferred locality — why does the distinction matter?
back:
Strict (internal traffic policy Local) is a requirement: no node-local endpoint means no traffic.
Preferred (topology-aware routing, traffic distribution) is a hint and falls back.
Only one of them can be the reason nothing is served, so treat requirements and hints differently in failure analysis.

front: A container is OOMKilled and starts again with the same Pod UID. Who restarted it?
back:
The kubelet, restarting the container in the existing sandbox under the Pod's restart policy.
No controller was involved and the Pod object never changed — which is why the Deployment shows nothing.

front: Same Pod UID with a higher {{c1::restartCount}} means a kubelet container restart; a {{c2::new UID}} means a controller created a replacement Pod.
back: ownerReferences and events then name which controller did it. Two fields separate the two cases without guesswork.

front: Why can a Job with a native sidecar finish?
back:
A native sidecar is an init container with restartPolicy: Always. It starts first, runs alongside the main containers, and the kubelet stops it once they finish.
That removes the classic never-exiting sidecar problem, where a proxy kept a Job running forever.

front: The independent knobs in a Job's result protocol
back:
Indexed completion — a stable index per unit of work.
backoffLimitPerIndex — retries bounded per index.
podFailurePolicy — classify outcomes, so a permanent exit code need not retry. Requires restartPolicy: Never on the template.
successPolicy — declare success before every index finishes.
activeDeadlineSeconds — cap total active time.

front: Why is a single global backoffLimit awkward for a large indexed Job?
back:
A few permanently broken indexes can exhaust a global budget and stop work that would have succeeded.
Per-index accounting lets healthy indexes finish and names the failed ones. The Job still ends Failed if any index is permanently failed, but you keep completed work and a named failure set instead of one shared retry budget wiping unfinished indexes mid-run.

front: A namespace is labelled Pod Security warn. What happens to a violating Pod?
back:
It is created, and the client gets a warning message.
Only enforce rejects. audit records to the audit log. Two of the three modes still admit the Pod.

front: Why “it passed Restricted admission” is not a security claim
back:
The standards are a bounded baseline, not all policy. Admission evaluated a spec, not a running process.
The runtime, RuntimeClass and kernel must actually enforce the mechanisms — and network, identity, image provenance and secret handling were never looked at.

front: securityContext settings that genuinely reduce runtime privilege
back:
Run as non-root; drop capabilities rather than add them; a seccomp profile; a read-only root filesystem; disallow privilege escalation.
These shape the process and runtime boundary. A label, annotation or controller revision carries no isolation property.

front: A Pod specifies a RuntimeClass for a sandboxed runtime. What must also be true?
back:
The named handler must be configured in the node's runtime on eligible nodes. RuntimeClass is a selector and a contract; the implementation lives on the node.
It can also add scheduling constraints and Pod overhead. Unconfigured, the Pod simply cannot run there.

front: What security property do Pod user namespaces primarily add?
back:
They remap container user IDs, so root inside the container is an unprivileged identity on the host.
That changes the kernel's identity mapping at the container boundary — a stronger property than a spec field, because it does not depend on the workload behaving.

front: After kubeadm init completes, what keeps the control plane running?
back:
The kubelet, realising the static Pod manifests kubeadm wrote. kubeadm writes PKI, kubeconfigs, manifests and bootstrap configuration, then exits.
There is no kubeadm daemon supervising the cluster afterwards.

front: A control-plane container is missing after a reboot. What is the highest-value first check?
back:
The static Pod manifest on disk and the kubelet — not the API.
If the kubelet cannot read or realise the manifest, the API object you see may be a stale mirror Pod: a reflection, not a running process.

front: Which separately versioned boundaries must you check during a Kubernetes upgrade?
back:
Control-plane components, kubelets, kube-proxy, the container runtime, the network plugin, and the API versions you still store — each has its own skew contract.
Treating the cluster as a single version is what turns an upgrade into an outage.

front: Does draining a node upgrade it?
back:
No. Drain cordons the node and attempts orderly eviction under its flags and policy. It normally respects PodDisruptionBudgets. DaemonSet and mirror Pods remain. Pods with local data need an explicit flag. You must still change the node configuration and binaries.
Conservative worker order: drain → change → verify the returning node → restore scheduling.

front: A ConfigMap changes. What happens automatically?
back:
Kubernetes refreshes normal ConfigMap volume projections eventually. A subPath mount does not refresh.
Environment values stay fixed for the process. Kubernetes does not restart the container or roll a Deployment only because the referenced ConfigMap changed. An application or controller can reload or roll workloads if configured to do so.

front: Is QoS class a field you set?
back:
No — it is derived from the CPU and memory requests and limits across all containers in the Pod.
One under-specified sidecar drops the whole Pod from Guaranteed to Burstable. If you expected Guaranteed and did not get it, check every container.

front: A valid HTTPRoute exists but nothing serves it. What has API acceptance proven?
back:
Only that the object was stored. A controller must still observe it and configure a proxy.
Read the route's status parents and conditions — that is where acceptance and resolution are reported. Existence is not attachment.

front: What Gateway API adds over Ingress
back:
Ownership separation. A platform team owns GatewayClass and Gateway — the infrastructure and its listeners. Application teams own Routes and attach them explicitly, with status reported on both sides.
Ingress puts both concerns in one object, usually mediated by annotations.

front: The scheduler found capacity, but node admission rejected the Pod on topology. Contradiction?
back:
No. The scheduler sums aggregate capacity; it does not prove a coherent NUMA placement.
Topology Manager is node-local and can refuse what looked feasible. Both components answered correctly — they answered different questions.

front: Which container gets exclusive CPUs under the static CPU Manager policy?
back:
One in a Guaranteed Pod requesting a whole number of CPUs.
Ask for a fraction and you stay in the shared pool, however important the workload. It is an exact rule, not a priority.

front: Is a CPU limit CPU isolation?
back:
No. A CFS quota caps how much time you get; a cpuset controls where you run. Different mechanisms, different axes.
Predictable latency also needs reserved system CPUs, NUMA-local memory and devices, IRQ placement, huge pages, and a runtime that preserves the intended cgroup layout.

front: Device plugin versus DRA — the architectural discriminator
back:
Device plugin advertises scalar extended resources through the kubelet. You request a count.
DRA publishes structured devices through API objects — ResourceSlices, DeviceClasses, ResourceClaims — so you can filter them, share them, and manage their lifecycle.
Both still need node-side preparation.

front: The DRA allocation handshake, in order
back:
Driver publishes inventory → scheduler allocates a matching device and selects a reachable node → kubelet and driver prepare the device on that node.
Availability precedes allocation; preparation happens only after node selection.

front: When is a ResourceClaimTemplate preferable to a named ResourceClaim?
back:
When the claim should live and die with the workload — the template is a factory, generating a claim per Pod and cleaning it up with the Pod.
A directly named claim can be shared between Pods or outlive any one of them. Choose by lifetime and sharing.

front: When does an aggregated API beat a CRD?
back:
Rarely, and only deliberately. CRDs already provide CRUD, watch and schema on the generic server. Status and scale are available when you enable them on the CRD.
Aggregation earns its operational cost only for behaviour the generic server cannot supply — custom storage, unusual subresources, or computed responses.

front: A watch {{c1::BOOKMARK}} carries no object change — it advances the resource version so you can resume; an HTTP {{c2::410 Gone}} means the history expired and you must rebuild state.
back: Bookmarks are an optimisation and optional. After a 410 there is no way to infer what you missed, so relist rather than guess.

front: Why can a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy be operationally safer than a webhook?
back:
It evaluates CEL in process — no Service, no DNS, no TLS trust, no response deadline on the API hot path.
It is not free: validation only (it cannot mutate), and matching scope, expression cost and failure policy are still deliberate decisions.

front: What can leader election guarantee — and what can it not?
back:
Can: one current Lease holder under API consistency, and failover once renewal stops and the duration expires.
Cannot: exactly-once external side effects. A deposed leader may still be mid-operation outside the cluster, so fencing or idempotency is a separate requirement.

front: A Pod is Pending with reason SchedulingGated. What do you investigate?
back:
Not a scheduling-capacity failure — the scheduler is deliberately skipping the Pod.
Read the named gates in the spec. Find which controller or admission rule added them. Identify the external prerequisite each gate waits on. Ask why that owner has not removed them.
Gates can be removed after creation but not newly added.

front: Where do you start diagnosing when the API server itself is not answering?
back:
Below Kubernetes. If an API load balancer exists, confirm what it thinks. Then static Pod manifests, the kubelet service, the runtime, certificates, sockets and host resources.
kubectl cannot diagnose the API server that makes kubectl work. Above that line, use object status, events and component health.

front: A ninety-second NotReady diagnosis
back:
Inspect conditions, taints and the node Lease → check host reachability and the clock → check the kubelet, including certificate and config errors → check the runtime and network plugin → preserve evidence before restarting.
The clock is the step people skip; skew produces certificate failures that look like something else.

front: What do Pod phase and common container waiting reasons each point at?
back:
Pending — admission, quota, scheduling or claims.
ContainerCreating (waiting reason on a Pending or Running Pod) — image, sandbox, network or mounts.
CrashLoopBackOff (waiting reason) — a process or probe failing repeatedly under the restart policy.
Running but not Ready — readiness, a dependency, or endpoint selection.
Phase names the Pod. Waiting reasons name the attempt. Events name what was tried. Do not call waiting reasons phases.

front: The compact troubleshooting algorithm
back:
1. State the transition you expected and what you observe.
  2. Identify the component that owns that transition.
  3. Read status, events and logs at that boundary.
  4. Compare with one adjacent healthy layer.
  5. Change one thing, and verify.
Every unit in the course is a way of answering step two quickly.

front: What is metadata.resourceVersion, and how must a client treat it?
back: A server version string used for concurrency and consistency. Pass it back unmodified. Compare order only for decimal values from the same API group and resource type. A stale value on update returns a conflict.

front: Your watch fails with status 410 Gone. What must the client do before it watches again?
back: Clear its local cache. Run a fresh get or list. Restart the watch from the resourceVersion that call returned. A server keeps only a short change history. BOOKMARK events reduce how often this happens.

front: Which CronJob concurrency policy skips a new Job when the previous run is still active?
back: Forbid. Allow runs overlap. Replace cancels the live Job and starts a new one.

front: You set maxSurge to 0 on a RollingUpdate Deployment. What else must be true?
back: maxUnavailable cannot be 0. At least one of the two must let the controller replace a Pod. During a template upgrade, Recreate waits for old-revision Pods to be removed before it creates new-revision Pods. It does not give an at-most guarantee after manual Pod deletion.

front: Why does apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 reject a CRD that has no OpenAPI schema?
back: v1 requires a structural schema. The API server uses it to validate and prune custom objects.

front: Which PriorityClass preemptionPolicy value stops this Pod from evicting lower-priority Pods?
back: Never. The default PreemptLowerPriority lets the scheduler evict lower-priority victims.

front: When does the kubelet start app containers if a Pod has several init containers?
back: After every init container exits 0, in spec order. A failed init restarts until it succeeds, unless restartPolicy is Never.

front: Which Service sessionAffinity value sends a client's later connections to the same backend Pod?
back: ClientIP. Connections from one client IP are sent to the same backend Pod for the configured affinity timeout. The default None provides no client affinity.

front: What does dnsPolicy: None change about a Pod's resolver?
back: The Pod ignores cluster DNS settings. You must set dnsConfig.nameservers. Extra nameservers under ClusterFirst merge; they do not replace cluster DNS.

front: If you omit dnsPolicy, the kubelet uses {{c1::ClusterFirst}}, not Default. Default copies the node's resolver.
back: Default is a named policy, not the field default. ClusterFirstWithHostNet is the cluster-DNS choice for hostNetwork Pods.

front: A PVC is deleted. Its PV has reclaim policy Retain. What is the volume's state?
back: The PV remains. Phase becomes Released. claimRef still names the old claim, so another PVC cannot bind until an admin clears it.

front: kubeadm-managed leaf certificates default to {{c1::1 year}}. A control-plane kubeadm upgrade renews them unless certificate renewal is disabled. CA certificates default to {{c2::10 years}}.
back: Check with kubeadm certs check-expiration. You can set other periods in ClusterConfiguration. Externally managed certificates need external renewal; the rotating kubelet client certificate is not in kubeadm certs check-expiration.

front: What changes after you set immutable: true on a ConfigMap?
back: You cannot change data or binaryData, and you cannot unset immutable. Delete and recreate. Watches for an immutable ConfigMap can close, which reduces load on kube-apiserver.

front: What must be true for status.qosClass to be Guaranteed?
back: Every container has CPU and memory request equal to its limit, both greater than zero. Equal pod-level CPU and memory also qualify when that feature is on.

front: You create an Ingress, but the cluster has no Ingress controller. What happens to the traffic?
back: Nothing routes. Only creating the resource has no effect; a controller must satisfy it. The Ingress API is frozen; the project recommends Gateway.

front: Which Topology Manager policy rejects a Pod when the merged hint is not preferred, but can accept a preferred alignment that spans multiple NUMA nodes?
back: restricted. The Pod is refused at kubelet admission and ends up Terminated; the scheduler does not retry. single-numa-node is stricter: it additionally requires alignment on one NUMA node.

front: In a Pod's spec.resourceClaims, what is the difference between resourceClaimTemplateName and resourceClaimName?
back: Template generates one ResourceClaim per Pod on demand and deletes it with the Pod. Name references a claim you created beforehand and keep alive yourself.

front: What does kubectl --as alice change, and which RBAC verb must you already hold?
back: The request authenticates as you, then evaluates authorization as alice. You need the impersonate verb on users.

front: In the common case, how does the control plane know a node is still alive?
back: The kubelet heartbeats by renewing its node's Lease spec.renewTime in kube-node-lease. Node status updates are separate and less frequent. Leader election reuses the API.

front: A node's Lease renewals stop arriving. What does the Ready condition become once the grace period passes?
back: Unknown. The node controller checks at --node-monitor-period; the grace period is --node-monitor-grace-period (default 50s). Pod eviction follows taints and the eviction controller.

front: To use the Node authorizer, a kubelet identifies as {{c1::system:node:<nodeName>}} in group {{c2::system:nodes}}.
back: When enabled, NodeRestriction limits a node identity to writes for its own Node and Pods bound to it, plus its documented label restrictions. TLS bootstrap issues the credential through a CertificateSigningRequest.

front: Which aggregated API behind kubectl top and HPA reports node and Pod CPU and memory only?
back: The Metrics API (metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1). metrics-server feeds it from the kubelet's resource metrics; it holds no history and no disk or network figures.

front: Server-side apply refuses your change to a field. What information does the error carry, and what must you do?
back: It names the field manager that owns the field. Reconcile your YAML with the live object, or force deliberately. update() does not join ownership.

front: A ResourceQuota counts CPU requests, and a LimitRange sets default CPU requests and limits. Why do Pods that declare no CPU now consume that quota?
back: Admission injects the defaults; every Pod gains CPU requests the quota counts. A violation is 403, not Pending.

front: You resized a container's resources in place. What happens to its QoS class?
back: Nothing. The class is fixed at Pod creation. Resize values must respect the original class: Guaranteed stays request equal to limit.

front: For a normal Service without publishNotReadyAddresses, an EndpointSlice endpoint is ready only when it is {{c1::serving}} and not {{c2::terminating}}.
back: With publishNotReadyAddresses: true, ready is always true. Proxies normally ignore terminating endpoints, but may use endpoints that are both serving and terminating when every available endpoint is terminating.

front: A Job Pod declares a helper in initContainers with restartPolicy: Always. How does the Job still complete?
back: A restartable init sidecar does not block Job completion. After every main container completes successfully, the Job can complete and the kubelet stops sidecars in reverse order.

front: Which Pod Security admission mode rejects a violating Pod outright, while the other two only record or warn?
back: enforce. audit appends to the API audit log; warn adds a response warning. They assess the resulting Pods, not the workload resource's wording.
